newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait draft budget $14.38 bln, deficit $3.85 bln.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait draft budget $14.38 bln, deficit $3.85 bln.

text.p: The Kuwait government is proposing a 4.37 billion dinar ($14.38 billion) budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) with a net deficit of 1.17 billion dinars ($3.85 billion), official figures showed on Monday.

The draft budget, obtained by Reuters, put expenditure at 4.37 billion dinars in addition to a 320 million dinar deposit in a fund for future generations, making the gross projected deficit for the next fiscal year 1.49 billion dinars.

The current 4.21 billion dinar budget carries a projected net deficit of 1.21 billion dinars and a gross deficit of 1.51 billion. By law, 10 percent of total revenues is placed in the overseas nest egg investment fund.
The budget proposal, which has to be approved by parliament and the head of state before it becomes law, put oil revenue at 2.56 billion dinars, almost unchanged from the previous year.
Non-oil revenue was unchanged at 645 million dinars.

Kuwait, which produces about two million barrels of oil a day, calculates oil revenue on a conservative average barrel price of $13. Officials and economists have said the actual deficit for the current fiscal year was expected to be halved due to stronger than forecast world oil prices.
Slightly more than half of the tiny state's oil earnings will be spent in 1997/98 on salaries which represent 29.5 percent of total expenditure.

More than 90 percent of Kuwaitis in the workforce are employed by the welfare state which offers them generous salaries and benefits unmatched by the private sector. Kuwait has a population of 710,000 Kuwaitis and 1.25 million foreigners.
But the Gulf Arab state, as part of a target to balance the budget by 2000 and a privatisation plan, hopes to employ less foreigners and encourage Kuwaitis to seek non-government jobs.
Salaries were put at 1.29 billion dinars in the draft budget compared with 1.25 billion dinars for the current fiscal year.

Independent sources estimate the size of the future generations fund at over $40 billion. It was worth more than $100 billion but the huge costs of the 1991 Gulf War, reconstruction following the seven-month Iraqi occupation and budget deficits depleted it to around $35 billion.
